keyVerseText: And there went out a champion out of the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath, of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span.
rootMeaning: The word בֵּנַיִם (bênayim) is the dual form of the Hebrew root בֵּין (bêyn), which fundamentally means 'between' or 'among.' This dual form literally refers to a 'double interval' or the space between two entities, specifically armies. Thus, beyond the common English gloss of 'champion,' the root sense emphasizes a position or role situated in the space separating opposing forces, highlighting a figure standing in the critical gap between conflict.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, בֵּנַיִם occurs only twice, and it is used to describe a 'champion,' specifically the notable Philistine warrior Goliath. The term carries the connotation of a man who occupies the space between two armies, serving as a formidable combatant or representative fighter. This usage consistently conveys both the literal spatial meaning and the metaphorical role of a champion who stands as a decisive figure in battle.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding בֵּנַיִם as rooted in the concept of 'between' enriches our grasp of biblical conflict, portraying champions not merely as strong warriors but as those who stand in the decisive gap on behalf of their people. This reflects the biblical theme of God raising up intercessors and deliverers who confront spiritual and physical opposition. For Christian faith, it foreshadows Christ as the ultimate champion who stands between humanity and sin, fighting on our behalf. Recognizing this word's original meaning invites believers to see Christ's victory as one that bridges the divide between God and man.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Samuel 17:4, the phrase 'a champion out of the camp of the Philistines' introduces Goliath as the man who stands in the space between the two armies, embodying the role of the feared warrior. The word בֵּנַיִם here highlights not just his physical stature but his function as the representative combatant occupying the critical interval between Israel and Philistia. This deepens the verse's portrayal of Goliath as the formidable obstacle whom David must face, symbolizing the spiritual and physical challenges confronting God's people.
